paragraphs.text: What I suppose troubles most people is the very thing that gladdens my heart. Most people, naturally enough, find it unpleasant to be crushed together, but for me it is the height of joy. A shepherd's eye rejoices when he sees his flock packed tight by its own numbers and spilling over the fold. The sheepfold is not small; it is the flock, thriving in its numbers, that makes the wide space narrow. Peter saw something like this around the Lord, and answered: "Master, the crowds are hemming you in and pressing upon you." Truly, as the divine Apostle says somewhere, this is what it means to be pressed yet not crushed: "In every way," he says, "we are pressed, but not crushed." But what word shall I bring out before such an assembly? Who will give me a voice louder than a trumpet, to sound over the crowd and lay up [?] in the ears of those gathered here? To which of the readings shall I turn my mind, to find a word suited to those present? Job is great, training our life in courage by his own example; great too is the author of Proverbs with his riddles. And what could one say of the holy Apostle? From those unutterable words which, he says, lie beyond human understanding, he has perhaps whispered to us too, through his teaching to the Ephesians, the hidden meaning of the cross, unveiling it in riddles. Other mysteries of this kind come from the psalmody: "for remembrance," "for an inscription on a pillar," and "for the winepresses." As we consider these words in the titles of the psalms read to us, we see that these riddles offer no small occasion for discourse. But I think it fitting to keep the discussion of these things for another time. What I want now is to find some word suited and appropriate to the present grace. What, then, is it? I know a certain

law of nature [?], engraved on the divine tablets themselves by the Lawgiver of nature, which commands us to repay our own parents with every good return, as far as our ability allows. "Honor," it says, "your father and your mother"; this is the first commandment with promises: "that it may be well with you." Now if this law comes first in its promise, and keeping it becomes the keeper's own gain (for the honor paid to parents returns to the one who has fulfilled the law), anyone with sense would do well to attend to this commandment, whose outcome is benefit and grace for the one who keeps it. The fathers of our flesh, however, having served their own generation for the time allotted them from the beginning, have no need of our honor. They departed this life long ago, so that such a law cannot be fulfilled, since those who would receive the kindness are no longer here. Yet the law commands us to win the promise by acting, for those who do nothing cannot have the prizes of those who act. What, then, should a man do when his parents are gone, if he longs for the promise and yet has no way to achieve what he strives for? Yes, what I see before me entirely resolves this difficulty. For when I look at you, I need not hunt for other fathers. You are my fathers, you who are fathers even of my fathers. For the homeland holds within itself the dignity of those who begot our begetters. What, then, shall we do to fulfill toward you the law of honor? A grateful and loving child renews his father's old age by his care and props up the frailty of his weakness, becoming everything to his father himself. So one may see the father growing young again in his child. An aged and trembling hand, resting on the strength of youth, enjoys the young man's vigor; and the step that already falters with shriveled limbs becomes active again through the child's zeal, held upright by his support. And if the old man's sight grows dim with time, through his child he becomes sharp-sighted again, led by the hand to the necessities of life. But you, our homeland, are not in such a state as to need any of these things. What, then, shall we do to obtain the blessing of the commandment? What gift shall we bring to please you, when you lack nothing good? Or would recounting your excellent qualities itself be the honor owed to you? Then this would be the time to tell of the things, of what kind and how many, in which your life takes pride. Or rather, we can not only tell of them but show them. But do you suppose I am going to speak of the common and obvious things: the fertility of the land, the abundance of crops,

and the river that divides the settlement? I mean the one that encloses its stream within the circuit of the plain and becomes a lake. Both before it forms the lake and afterward, it is cut into channels for the needs of each inhabitant, passes through the groves and meadows it so skillfully tends, and supplies countless delights to those who live there, dividing itself to meet every wish of the city's inhabitants. Let others speak of these things, whose eloquence serves them for grandeur and wins some distinction among the well trained, as they increase the praise of the homeland from such themes. And let some worldly man, who knows how to judge the goods of this life, add to his praises, if he likes, the other river as well. I mean our neighbor, which because of its size is counted among the famous rivers of the world. It begins in our territory and in due course flows past the city, contributing no small grace of its own to its beauty and to the support of its life. And if one must list founders, or glorify the inhabitants' descent from colonists, or add to our story the achievements of warlike hands (trophies, battles, and the marvels of valor, all that the sons of historians have stored up in books), these things are far from our chorus. For a Christian discourse is ashamed to praise the lovers of Christ for things outside the faith; that would be like glorifying the champion's shadow in preference to his trophies. So let our discourse turn to what is before us and set your fruit before our eyes. Let the beauties of the world be silent, even if such a subject for praise is more than plentiful. For the divinely inspired word does not regard as great or worthy of wonder the whole heaven, which is the fairest and greatest of all things in creation, nor the rays of the heavenly lights, nor the breadth of the earth, nor anything else among the elements that underlie the universe. I have been taught by the divine command not to be moved to wonder at anything that passes away. If, then, all heaven and earth will pass away, and the form of this world is passing away entirely, as the Apostle says, how could anyone think it fitting to put forward the fertility of land and water as grounds for praise? Even if your region possesses such advantages of the earth more than others, the discourse knows to pass them by as nothing in comparison with your true goods. Let us therefore turn our praises to things more precious by nature. These will no longer be shown us by words; we can look upon the very crown of your goods. For who does not know your fruit, that you have grown the ear of grain of the martyrs, this rich ear, swelling beyond thirtyfold in the number of its grains?

Look at this holy field: from here come the sheaves of the martyrs. If you want to know which field I mean, do not look far beyond what is in front of you. What is the place that holds this assembly? What does the yearly turning of the cycle tell you? What stories has the memorial of this day come bringing you? Are there not, as the Prophet says, speeches and words whose voices are not only heard, but tell of the wonders more forcefully than any words? If you look at the place, it says that it is itself the martyrs' stadium; if you consider the day, it proclaims the martyrs' crown like a loud-voiced herald. I seem to hear the day crying out: "One day takes pride in the creation of the heavenly lights, another in the heaven, and another exults in the fashioning of the earth. But for me the wonders of the martyrs are adornment enough. It is enough for me to pride myself on the beauty of their crowns; it is enough to glory in their trophies over the devil. What stories have come about in me! What an increase came to the angels through me! What fruit the earth gave to God! What a planting the Lord planted in me!" From it nearly the whole world has been planted with shoots from the branches that grew here, just as a flourishing vine produces other vines from itself and yet remains unfailing. These and similar things the grace of the day seems to proclaim, and the place of assembly proclaims others like them. But what am I to do before so great a people, when I am weak-voiced and slow of tongue, and can scarcely make myself heard by those standing near me, while the noise drowns out my words? I would gladly have lingered over the good stories: how the noble company of the Forty, having shared their contest, has also made its settlement shared everywhere; how they are distributed everywhere and dwell as guests in many places together. And so no one who has received a portion of the grace of the relics has failed to receive the presence of the martyrs in their entirety. For since they all became one in the Lord, through one of them they take up residence with their whole company. But how can I avoid wronging the discourse if I keep silent about the beginning of their story? What, then, is the beginning? A youth that was good and admired, a faith of the highest excellence, on account of which they were all chosen, outstanding in beauty, like young saplings in stature in the flower of their prime. Do you see how my voice is thrown into confusion by the din, and my words cut off by the noise, so that, storm-tossed as on a sea surging with the voices of the people, we must of necessity flee to the calm harbor of silence? But if by God's grace we have leisure for the second part of the discourse, with a quiet audience, what has now been left out will be completed with God's help. To him be glory for ever and ever.

Yesterday the martyrs called the people to themselves; today they come unbidden as guests to the house of the Church. There is a custom among those who dine together that these recurring banquets are given by the guests to one another in turn. So we too must repay the martyrs with the same contribution to the meal. But since our supply of eloquence is poor, it is right to entertain them with their own leftovers: yesterday's hosts, today's guests. For even a small portion from a rich table is enough to provide a great feast, when the leftover is of such a kind. What, then, is this leftover? You surely remember where we were in the discourse when that welcome and delightful din of the great crowd gathered here drowned out what was being said. That living sea of the church, flooding with the numbers pouring in, surged with the pressure of those continually forcing their way in, and imitated the real sea in its roar too, as though dashing the crash of its waves against our very ears. At what point, then, we left the discourse, storm-tossed by the din, you surely remember, you who make a practice of keeping the martyrs in memory. The thread of the discourse was, I think, this: those chosen for this contest were not ordinary men, nor some mixed and nameless rabble who set out from lowly occupations and were raised to this dignity. First, because of their fine physique, they surpassed the rest in beauty, strength, and abundant vigor, and so were enrolled on the military lists. After that, distinguished by a virtuous life and sober conduct, they were perfected and received the grace of martyrdom as a kind of prize and reward for valor. And if you like, so that we may enjoy it more, let us take up the whole story of the martyrs in order, setting before the present audience, as it were, the [?]

There was an old military unit in the neighboring city, stationed in front of the whole nation against the attacks of the barbarians. Because of a divine manifestation that had occurred among them earlier, they cultivated faith more than tactics. And perhaps it is not out of place to relate in passing one achievement of these men's faith. Once, when war had broken out between them and the barbarians, all the strategic positions had been seized beforehand by the enemy army, and the sources of water had fallen into the enemy's power, they came into extreme danger. This happened either through the inexperience of those commanding our side, or through some higher and more divine dispensation, so that the difference between Christians and foreigners might be shown all the more clearly by it. They did not know what to do in their situation, and their helplessness was great, for no spring or stream of water appeared anywhere in the place, and they were in danger of yielding to the

enemy, forced to surrender by thirst. Then the noble men set aside the help that comes from arms and resolved to call upon the invincible and unconquerable Ally in their danger. Leaving in the camp those who had not yet received the faith, they withdrew by themselves and imitated the miracle worked in the time of Elijah the prophet, asking with one common and concerted voice that they be delivered from their calamity, helpless as they were. They prayed, and at once the prayer became deed. While they were still kneeling, a cloud, carried from somewhere by a violent wind, came to rest high above the enemy camp. Then it crashed with extraordinary thunder, kindled fiery lightning against those below, and poured down water more abundantly than rivers. For the enemy, the continual thunderbolts and the force of the downpour brought about total destruction; but for those who had drawn up their battle line through prayer it sufficed for both purposes, for victory over their opponents and for relief from thirst, since the flowing torrents supplied them abundantly with drink. It was into this unit, then, that our band of soldiers was enrolled. They too were confirmed in the faith by those stories and brought up in the same practices, and they rose to such greatness of spirit that their surpassing virtue stirred up envy against them. For just as we learned from the passages of the story of Job just read to us, the adversary of human life regarded Job's good repute as an injury to himself, and therefore demanded him for torment, because Job grieved him by being true, righteous, and blameless. In the same way the one who preys upon the good looked with an evil eye on these great contestants and could not bear to see the gray hairs of character in youthful years. He saw the flower of their bodies adorned with self-control. He saw an armed chorus, as it were, dancing for God through their soldiering: fair to look upon, fierce of eye, proud of spirit, swift of foot, abundant in strength, well proportioned in limb, and, among all their advantages, a virtue of soul that outshone their bodily blessings. He who walks to and fro throughout the world walks among them too in his envy. He saw not one true man but a divine company of so many men, all of them true, righteous, and God-fearing, and he demands them too for his own purpose. First he becomes counselor to the idol-mad commander of the army, persuading him that he could win victory over the barbarians in no other way than by first sacrificing those who worship the name of Christ. When these men very quickly made themselves known by their good confession and went over of their own accord toward perfection through suffering, the Enemy declined to inflict immediate death by the sword, as being too humane; instead he crushed them in iron chains

On the Forty Martyrs.

and made this the beginning of their punishment. But for them even the chain was an adornment, and a lovely and delightful sight to Christian eyes: a chosen youth so many in number, outstanding in beauty, taller than other men, all fitted together in the same chain, like a crown or a necklace with pearls of equal size set in a circle. Such were the saints, united by faith and bound tightly to one another by their chains. Each was beautiful in himself, and they added to one another's beauty. So it is with the wonders of heaven, when in a clear, pure sky the stars embroider one another's loveliness, each contributing its own gleam to the common adornment of the heavens. Such was the sight of the saints: truly, as the prophet Ezekiel says somewhere, "the appearance of torches whirling together." The discourse lingers lovingly on the beauty of their youth. For it knows, as Wisdom says, how to infer the hidden beauty from the greatness and beauty of created things, since the purity of the soul shone through the visible body, and the visible man was a dwelling worthy of the invisible. How beautiful, then, was that sight to those who saw it! Beautiful, I say, to those willing to see what is beautiful, beautiful to the angels, beautiful to the powers above the world; but bitter to the demons and to all who embraced the ways of demons. These were men (if indeed they were men, who rose so far above the greatness of nature), soldiers of Christ, men-at-arms of the Holy Spirit, champions of the faith, towers of the divine city. They mocked every punishment of torture, every assault of terror, every onset of threats, as childish folly, as though what they surrendered to the torments were not their bodies but the shadows of their bodies. Wrestling down the flesh with the flesh, and despising all the terrors of tyrants through their contempt for death, they showed themselves loftier than human measure. How well they had trained themselves for bodily victories! How well they transferred their experience of warfare to the battle against the devil! They did not arm their hands with the sword, nor hold up a wooden shield, nor protect themselves with a bronze helmet and greaves. Instead they took up the whole armor of God, which the general of the Church, the divine Apostle, describes: shield, breastplate, helmet, and sword. So equipped, they advanced against the opposing power. Heavenly grace was their general; the general of the devil's battle line was he who has the power of death. The field of battle was the court of the bloodthirsty. There they met and fought it out, the one side skirmishing with threats, the other defending itself with endurance. The terms offered by their opponents were these: forswear your faith in the Lord, or be punished with death.

The champions answered that they would hold to their confession until death. In response, fire was threatened, and the sword, and the pit, and every other name of punishment. Against all of these a single cry was heard: Christ, confessed in the mouths of the saints. This was the blow that struck their opponents. This was the spear-point they held out against the enemy. By this cry the Adversary was wounded [?]. This is the stone slung by David's hand, which strikes [?] the Adversary's helmet. For the confession of Christ becomes the sling of the good soldier. The Enemy falls and is left headless. But my speech has bolted and been carried away. It leaps beyond its bounds and ventures into things that cannot be spoken. It is led on to speak as though it had become [?] a witness of things invisible, and to say that when that cry boldly confessed Christ, there was applause above and praise from the holy angels. The citizens of the heavenly city acclaimed the achievement and applauded it, and the whole festal assembly in heaven rejoiced. For what a theatre was then set up for the angels in the world of men! What a contest they saw between the devil and men, they who are the spectators of our life! How opposite it was to that first wrestling match, when the serpent threw Adam! Then man could not withstand a single assault of the Evil One, brought against him by means of an attractive color and a bait. At once he fell, and the fall overthrew him. But here all the Enemy's holds proved idle and useless. He held out hopes, and they trampled on them; he threatened terrors, and they laughed at them. Only one thing was fearful to them: to be separated from Christ. Only one thing was good: to be with Christ alone. Everything else was a joke, a shadow, nonsense and the phantoms of a dream. That is why my speech dares to approach things no eye has seen. It says that the whole power above the world exulted in the achievement of the athletes. My speech grows bold against what should not be dared. It dares to describe what lies beyond the world: that while these deeds were being done here, in the struggle against the adversaries, the just judge of the games held out the crowns for victory, the chief commander of the divine host made ready the prizes for the victors, and the Holy Spirit welcomed them with gifts of every kind. For since it was faith in the Trinity that was confessed, grace was measured out to them in return from the Trinity. And what was this grace? It was this very thing: that they were shown to stand higher than the first contestants, Adam, I mean, and Eve. Those two brought human nature down through sin while it was still standing. These men raised it up again through their endurance as it lay in the fall of those who came before. Those two were driven out of paradise onto the earth. These were moved from here up to paradise. Those two armed death against themselves (for "the weapon of death is sin," as Scripture says). These, by their courage, made useless the death that sin had armed, blunting the point of its sting by enduring their

sufferings, so that one may rightly say, "Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O Hades, is your victory?" What is more wretched than the fruit of a tree? What is cheaper than wood? Yet a fruit tinged with attractive color and the pleasure of taste caused the grace of paradise to be despised. To these great contestants, however, not even the sun itself seemed sweet. They willingly gave up even the sun, so as not to fall away from the true light. What does Scripture say about Eve (for I am drawn on, even beyond what is needed, to find fault with our first parents)? "She saw," it says, "that it was pleasing to the eyes and lovely to taste." Then they exchanged paradise for the charm of these things. But for these men [?] the things that delighted the eye and the taste were the sky, the sun, the earth, people, homeland, mothers, brothers, friends, relatives and companions of their own age. What is sweeter to see than these? What is more precious to taste? You children know the love you have for your parents. You fathers know the affection you have for your children. You who see know how sweet the sun is. You who love your brothers are not unaware of the natural bond between brothers. You young people understand the delight that comes from your companions, and how much they sweeten your life. But to those men all these things were hostile and foreign. There was only one good: Christ. They renounced everything in order to gain him. Their time in chains was not short, and as the punishment dragged on, the saints' longing to be perfected grew along with it. People who train for bodily fitness go confidently to the contests once they have gained enough strength in the trainer's school. In the same way, these men were thoroughly trained in piety by their chains and their prison, and so they advanced to the crown of the contests. The course of my speech has come to the end, or rather to the summit of the whole achievement. This was the time, and these were the days of the contest: this prelude to Easter, the mystery of the holy Forty Days. Forty are our days of atonement, and equal in number are the crowns of the saints. Perhaps I seem to you superfluous and long-winded, telling you about your own wonders among yourselves and regaling your ears with what is already yours? Still, so that my speech may not pass you by and leave things incomplete, we too will run with the saints to the end of their contests. There was a hard frost on that day. You certainly need no one to tell you what that frost was like. You can guess from the present day: a frost that pierces even through the hair. You know how extreme it is, both you who visit these parts and you who were born here, and you need no speech to teach you. But someone else might describe the marvels your winters work: how ever-flowing rivers stand still, as the frost resists their current and turns the waves to stone, and how the neighboring lake needs some markers to be recognized as a lake at all, since the frost has turned it

into dry land, so that people who wish to do so commonly ride horses over its waves. I know that the local people often get water from fire as well. They break off a lump of water and melt it in the fire as though it were bronze or iron, and so make the stone into water. Such was the weather at the time of the contest. The evil had taken on an unnatural severity from the north winds, as one can hear from those who tell of these wonders. So the martyrs had splendidly and publicly proclaimed the name of the Lord, and by this proclamation had already shown themselves crowned. As they were going on to be made perfect through death, this was the form of contest devised for them. The tyrant issued an order: the athletes were to be punished with the frost. O how weak are words and thoughts! How far my speech falls short of what it deserves! An order of death, and frost, and punishment, and the expectation of such torment, and yet the blessed young men took their places for punishment with laughter, play and cheerfulness. The athletes raced toward their suffering, a holy and eager race, each striving to seize the crown of confession first. Their eagerness matched the victory. No one was seen lagging behind in zeal. With one accord they all took over this place as though it were then a public bath with time to spare, and as if they too were about to wash their bodies clean in the bath, they readily laid aside the tunics that covered them. All of them repeated the words of Job: "Naked we came into the world; naked we will depart to the one who brought us in. We brought nothing into the world, and we must carry nothing out. Or rather, though we came in naked, we will depart full of the treasures that come from the good confession." Saying these things and encouraging one another with such words, they gave their bodies to the frost. The nature of the elements was mastered by the frost, but the nature of the martyrs was not enslaved. Or rather, their nature suffered what is natural to it and felt the pains, but the athletes' greatness of spirit fought on even against nature itself. Their strength dissolved little by little, withering and wasting away in the frost, but the vigor of their souls grew greater. The bloom of their bodies darkened, their beauty faded, and the healthy color of their flesh withered away. Their fingers dropped off, cut away bit by bit by the frost, and all their limbs and senses were crushed by the bitter cold. For their flesh gradually turned livid, swelled, split open at the limbs and fell away from the bones, and they felt the sufferings of death while still conscious. And so death crept forward on them little by little and was drawn out over three days. For as long as their

consciousness lasted, they remained in the rank where they had been stationed from the beginning, and in everything they proved victors over the adversary. But who could tell worthily what came next? What speech will sketch that divine procession, when the holy bodies were carried in procession on wagons to the fire? Who will tell how, in place of the one whom the devil stole, the jailer was brought into the number by grace? Who will tell me about that mother, the worthy root of a martyr? Her son was left behind by the executioner because he was still breathing, and so he was not lifted onto the wagon with the others. When she saw the executioner's "kindness" toward the champion, she could not bear the insult. She reviled him for cutting the athlete off from his fellow contestants. Then she stood beside the martyr. He was already numb and frozen motionless. She saw him held by a cold and feeble breath, alive only enough to feel the pain, looking up at his mother with a dim and fading gaze, signing to her with his dead and limp hand, comforting her and urging her to bear it nobly. When the mother saw this, did she feel anything a mother would? Was her heart moved? Did she tear her tunic, or throw herself around her child to warm his wasted body in her warm arms? Far from it! Even to suggest such a thing is absurd. Truly we know the tree by its fruit: a rotten tree cannot bear good fruit. Since the fruit of martyrdom is good, praise the mother of a noble son, the woman saved through childbearing, as the Apostle says. For by presenting such fruit to God she made a defense for the common nature of women. "You are not my child," she says. "You are not the offspring of my labor pains. You received God, and you were born according to God. You received power to become a child of God. Run to your Father, so that you are not left behind by your companions, so that you do not come second to the crown, so that you do not leave a mother's prayer unfulfilled. You will not grieve your mother if you become crowned, a victor and a bearer of trophies." Saying this, she strengthened herself beyond nature, or rather she was strengthened by the Spirit. With her own hands she laid her son on the cart with the rest, and with a radiant face she escorted the athlete in the procession. And what came after this? The saints contended in the open air. They sanctified even the fire by joining it, becoming fuel for the flame. They brought a blessing to the water as well. Through everything the divine sayings were fulfilled. The three young men call on frost and heat to join in the common hymn of praise: the frost through the freezing, the heat through the burning. Then they passed through fire and water. But my speech wishes to pass over these things as well known, and now, at a fitting time, to examine one of the questions raised earlier.

When man was banished from paradise, the flaming sword that turns was set to guard the entrance. The reason for this provision on God's part was that man should not reach the tree of life, touch it and live on forever. You surely remember the questions that were raised. You probably also remember what we found in answer to the question. But if we were to go over everything again from the beginning and take up the whole discussion, it would run on longer than the present occasion allows. This was the question: If paradise cannot be entered even by the saints because of the turning sword, and the athletes are shut out of paradise, what promise is left for which they take on the contests of piety? And will they have less than the thief, to whom the Lord said, "Today you will be with me in paradise"? Yet the thief did not come to the cross willingly. But when he came near salvation, the sharp and clever thief saw the treasure, seized his chance and plundered life. He used his thief's skill well and with good aim when he said, "Lord, remember me in your kingdom." Is he then judged worthy of paradise, while the flaming sword bars the saints from entering? Surely the question carries its own answer. This is why Scripture did not show the sword always standing face to face with those who enter, but made it a turning sword. To the unworthy it appears facing them, but for the worthy it turns and comes to be at their back, opening for them an unhindered entrance to life. They have now come inside, having passed through the flame unharmed by the boldness of their contests. May we too pass through it without fear and come to be inside paradise, strengthened by their intercession for the good confession of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory to the ages of ages. Amen.
